The Holi I was eleven, Simran twice pushed ahead of me in the colour-stall queue. The second time I shoved her so hard she fell in the wet colour and scraped her hand. Her mother came running. And I heard myself say, "She asked for it. She kept cutting the line."
I believed it. In my head she had made me do it.
My father didn't shout. He just said, "Nilesh, she cut the line. What did you do?" I said, "I pushed her." "And who is responsible for the push?" I didn't want to answer.
It took me years to see what I'd done. I had turned Simran into the cause so I didn't have to feel bad. The line-cutting was hers. The push was mine.
— Nilesh

Student counsellor's note, by Amandeep
Sudha, second-year B.Com, came in today, very low. Last week she paid a "registration fee" for an online internship that turned out to be fake. The company's page vanished. When she told her flatmates, one said, "How could you be so stupid? Everyone knows those are scams." Her cousin said, "You should have been smarter." She said to me, "I feel like an idiot. I lost the money and now I feel ashamed too."
I told her plainly: the people who built the fake page chose to cheat her. That is on them. Scams are designed to fool careful people.
What I did next: we sat together and she called her bank's helpline from my office to report it, and we filed a complaint on the national cyber-crime portal. I've asked her to come back on Monday, and I gave her the number of the college's legal aid cell.

Thursday night
I got scammed. A man called saying he was from a courier company, that my parcel was stuck and I had to pay a small fee to release it. I clicked the link and entered my card details. Two withdrawals followed within minutes.
I told Bidisha, and the first thing she said was, "Bhavna, how could you fall for that? You're supposed to be smart." I felt my face burn. I went to the bathroom and cried. It wasn't just the money. It was feeling stupid on top of it.
An hour later Bidisha knocked. "I'm sorry. That was a horrible thing to say. You didn't do this, they did." Then she sat with me while I called the bank to block the card, and we filed a complaint on the cyber-crime helpline. The bank man said they see hundreds of these a week.
I still feel shaky. But not stupid any more.
Bhavna

Neelam's term essay was excellent. Too excellent. The style didn't match any of her earlier work. When I asked her about it, she admitted she had paid someone online to write it. Then she said, "Sir, it's one essay. People are buying entire degrees these days. Some students pay for exams to be written. This is nothing compared with that."
I noticed she didn't mention her own values once. Her standard was the worst example she could find.
I asked, "Forget the people buying degrees. When you started college, what kind of student did you want to be?" She looked at the desk for a long time. "The kind who writes her own work." "So what does this essay say about you, by your own standard?" She didn't answer, but her eyes filled.
What I did next: I gave her two weeks to write a new essay herself, and told her I'd help with the outline if she came to office hours.

Tuesday
I paid a senior to write my chemistry lab report. I told myself it was fine. Binita's cousin knows someone who bought an entire degree certificate. There's a whole shop near the station that sells project reports. Compared with that, one lab report is nothing. I'm hardly a criminal.
Then today in the lab, sir asked me to explain my own conclusion to the class. I couldn't. I stood there with my face burning while Binita stared at her notebook.
Tonight I keep thinking. Why was I measuring myself against a man who buys a degree? I never wanted to be him. When I joined this course, I wanted to actually understand chemistry. Dad took a loan for my fees.
By my own standard, not the station shop's, what I did was cheating.
Tomorrow I'll tell sir I didn't write it and ask to redo it.
Chaitanya

passage: I'm Kalyani, and I sit beside Zubin at the travel company. Last Friday, he was filling in his expense report for the Jaipur trip. I saw him paste in two taxi receipts, then pause. passage: Nikita, you're asking how I stayed straight in forty years of office work? Let your Hansa Ajji tell you. During Durga Puja, when I was ten, someone ate half the sandesh meant for the pandal. It was me. I told Ma, "Bhavna ate them." My cousin Bhavna was seven and cried.

— Anirban

Friday, after the biology test
I got 14 out of 40.
Last night I read through the notes twice, very fast. Every page looked familiar. Mitochondria, yes. Osmosis, yes. I remember thinking, "I know all this." I went to sleep at ten, feeling calm.
Then this morning, question 3: "Explain how osmosis happens in root hair cells." I stared at it. I knew the word. I knew the diagram was on page 12. But I couldn't write a single sentence about how it actually works.
Avni got 35. She said she didn't reread the notes at all. She covered them and tried to explain each topic out loud to her sister.
So "it looks familiar" isn't the same as "I understand it". My brain was fooling me with that feeling.
Next test, I'm going to cover the page and explain it first.
Ojas

passage: The bus from Chikmagalur town to Preeti's village took forty minutes, and every morning before the history exam, she flipped through her notes on the way. Chapter after chapter looked familiar. The Mauryas. The Guptas. The trade routes. "I know all this," she told Bhupen, her neighbour, who sat beside her with his own books. Bhupen closed her notebook. "Then tell me: why did the Mauryan empire decline?" Preeti opened her mouth. "Because... there were... reasons." "Which reasons?" She laughed nervously. "I read that page three times!" "Reading and knowing aren't the same." Preeti stared at the fields rushing past. She felt suddenly less sure. On the day of the exam, the question came, word for word. She wrote four vague lines. When the marks came, she got 22 out of 60. She was stunned. On the bus home, she asked Bhupen to quiz her every morning from then on.
